claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloy stability at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable, disordered solid-solution phase.
Configurational entropy of mixing influences formation of the stable, disordered solid solution.
Atomic-scale interactions among the constituent elements influence formation of the stable, disordered solid solution.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy has a disordered solid-solution structure.
The proposed intervention is annealing at 500–1000 °C under an inert-gas atmosphere.
Atomic-scale interactions among constituent elements lead to a stable, disordered solid-solution phase.
Relative to conventional low-configurational-entropy alloys, the high-entropy nanoalloy will have improved structural and chemical stability after annealing.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit reduced grain growth relative to the baseline.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit increased oxidation resistance relative to the baseline.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit minimal phase segregation.
Conventional alloys used as the baseline have low configurational entropy of mixing.
The prediction is limited to alloys containing 5–10 principal elements and annealed at 500–1000 °C.
The exact relationship between configurational entropy of mixing and stability is not well established.
The roles of lattice distortion and electronic effects in stability are not fully understood.
The proposed test compares high-entropy nanoalloys having different configurational entropies after high-temperature annealing.
